entities.summary:
Mattan I ruled Tyre from 840 to 832 BC, succeeding his father Baal-Eser II.

Mattan I was a king of the city-state of Tyre in ancient Phoenicia. His reign marked the beginning of a new era for Tyre, which would go on to play a significant role in the Mediterranean trade and politics of the time.

Under Mattan's leadership, Tyre experienced a period of growth and prosperity, with its strategic location making it an attractive destination for merchants and traders from all over the ancient world. The city's economy flourished, and its culture became more diverse as people from different regions came to live and trade there.

Despite his success, Mattan I faced challenges during his reign, including conflicts with neighboring cities and the Egyptian Empire.

One of the most notable legacies of Mattan I was the construction of a new temple dedicated to the god Baal, which would become a symbol of Tyre's power and religious devotion. The temple's design and architecture were influenced by the Phoenician style, but also showed signs of Egyptian influence due to the city's extensive trade connections with Egypt.

The legacy of Mattan I continued long after his death, as his successors built upon the foundations he laid for Tyre's growth and prosperity. His reign marked an important turning point in the history of Tyre, cementing its status as a major power in the ancient Mediterranean world.

Mattan I died at the age of 68, leaving behind a legacy that would be remembered for centuries to come.
